Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach is a self-evolving rubric framework that evaluates and enhances LLM agent skill-use across four process dimensions (selection, following, composition, reflection), providing better supervision than outcome-only methods by distinguishing process quality from accidental task success.
AI.motivation: Final verifier success is too coarse for evaluating agentic skill-use because agents may succeed through trial and error despite selecting distractor skills, skipping steps, composing workflows incorrectly, or omitting final checks in realistic skill repositories with overlapping skills.
AI.method: SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. The external verifier is kept as a separate outcome signal. Evolved rubrics serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories.
AI.result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: Process-grounded rubrics are superior to coarse outcome signals for both evaluating and training LLM agents in realistic, overlapping skill repositories.

title: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

AI.tldr: AUF (Acceptance-Unaware Fixation) is a training modification for block-style speculative decoding drafters that truncates the cross-entropy loss to only supervise tokens up to the first predicted failure, rather than the full block. This simple change improves average emitted length from 2.40 to 2.61 on DFlash and 2.56 to 2.68 on Domino for Qwen3-8B, with no inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding's block drafters are trained with full-block cross-entropy that supervises every token position equally, yet during inference, tokens after the first rejection are discarded. This training-inference mismatch wastes capacity on positions that never matter.
AI.method: AUF (Acceptance-Unaware Fixation) modifies the cross-entropy loss for mask-only block drafters by truncating the support to only include tokens up to and including the drafter's first predicted failure. Unlike prior acceptance-aware objectives that reweight the full-block loss, AUF simply removes the loss beyond the failure point—no auxiliary objectives, verifier rollouts, or inference changes.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B with fixed drafter backbones, AUF increases DFlash's average emitted length τ from 2.40 to 2.61 (gain on all 6 benchmarks), and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56→2.68). The decay-only baseline achieves higher token accuracy on the shared block mask but worse decoding; standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert once AUF truncates the support.
AI.conclusion: Simply truncating the CE loss to the first predicted failure point effectively concentrates supervision on the accepted prefix, improving speculative decoding throughput without any inference-side changes or auxiliary components.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE is the first tool for assessing complexity in both prompt and code layers of LLM-integrated applications. Using a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism, it generates 52 candidate metrics across 25 complexity dimensions. After validation against 118 components from 18 repositories, only 10 metrics survive, with 7 being newly introduced "structural breadth" metrics that measure distinct structural elements (LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates) rather than volume. Prompt-layer metrics remain significant even when controlling for code-level metrics, establishing prompt complexity as an independent dimension.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity metrics operate solely at the code level and fail to capture behavioral logic originating from the prompt layer in LLM-integrated applications.
AI.method: HECATE uses Prompt-as-Specification (a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism) to treat prompts as behavioral specifications. It generates 52 candidate metrics grounded in 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies, then validates them against 118 components from 18 open-source repositories using maintenance activity from version history as a proxy for complexity.
AI.result: Only 10 metrics withstand significance testing after controlling for code size. Seven are newly introduced "structural breadth" metrics (counting structurally distinct elements like LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates). Of three surviving conventional metrics, RFC shows breadth-oriented character while Halstead N and V survive only as residual size effects. Prompt-layer metrics remain significant when the strongest code-level metric is added as covariate.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity is an independent dimension of software complexity in LLM-integrated applications. The two best-performing metrics generalize beyond the training set, validated on 20 components from 6 held-out repositories, confirming their predictive power for maintenance effort.

title: ContextSniper: AntTrail's Token-Efficient Code Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair
summary: Large language model agents can repair real repository issues, but they often spend large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs. This paper presents ContextSniper, AntTrail's token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair. As the coding specialization of AntTrail's broader agent memory engine, ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: it retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. We evaluate ContextSniper on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code, using 50 task runs per host-agent condition. ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw, and reduces total token use by 38.9% and estimated cost by 27.3% for Claude Code. Submitted-resolution rates decrease slightly, from 26.0% to 24.0% for OpenClaw and from 32.0% to 30.0% for Claude Code. ContextSniper's pilot testing scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper

AI.tldr: ContextSniper is a token-efficient code memory layer that reduces total token usage by 38.9-51.5% and cost by 27.3-36.4% for LLM-based repository repair agents, with only a 2% absolute drop in resolved rates (SWE-bench Lite).
AI.motivation: LLM agents for repository repair waste large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs.
AI.method: ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Lite: OpenClaw — 51.5% token reduction, 36.4% cost reduction, resolution rate 26.0%→24.0%; Claude Code — 38.9% token reduction, 27.3% cost reduction, resolution rate 32.0%→30.0%.
AI.conclusion: ContextSniper substantially improves token and cost efficiency for LLM repair agents with minimal degradation in resolution performance, and its pilot scripts are open-sourced.

title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
summary: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, these external dependencies introduce novel attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks show that maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. These threats reflect a deeper issue: the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning. Inspired by prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble), ElephantAgent extends this protection to the evolving contextual state of agentic systems. We define the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's entire context (e.g., tool state and memory). Before processing each query, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Using replicated trusted hardware, ElephantAgent maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detects out-of-band state tampering. To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

AI.tldr: ElephantAgent is a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against tool/memory poisoning in agentic systems by recomputing and verifying digests of the contextual state before each query, using replicated trusted hardware and a linearizable ledger for tamper detection, plus Historical Traceability for post-hoc audit and recovery.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems rely on external tools and persistent memory, which introduce novel attack surfaces (tool/memory poisoning) that can covertly bias agent behavior. There is a lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution.
AI.method: ElephantAgent defines the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context (tool state, memory). Before each query, it recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. It uses replicated trusted hardware to maintain a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions, detecting out-of-band tampering. For in-band semantic abuse, it provides Historical Traceability for conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.
AI.result: The paper presents a defense mechanism against contextual state poisoning in agentic systems, extending prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble) to protect the evolving contextual state of agents.
AI.conclusion: ElephantAgent enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning, providing both tamper detection (via digest verification and linearizable ledger) and recovery (via Historical Traceability) for agentic systems.

title: A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Long term memory lets LLM agents act as persistent assistants, but user facts change. A useful memory system must know what is true now, what used to be true, and what changed. We study \emph{ghost memory}, a state coordination failure in which old, current, and transition facts coexist in the memory bank, remain mixed during retrieval, and mislead the answer model. We argue that memory systems should be understood and optimized from three levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer time resolution. We propose ATMA, a state aware overlay for existing memory systems. ATMA keeps superseded and transition records in the bank, builds evidence packets for the query's requested state view, and exposes current, historical, and transition labels to QA. We further call for decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer level failures, since final QA accuracy can hide where ghost memory occurs. To make this failure measurable, we build LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict heavy benchmark for ghost memory, and evaluate on LoCoMo for long conversation generalization. On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. The gains are host dependent, but they indicate that explicit state roles can reduce memory failures hidden by final QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "ghost memory" in LLM agents—where old, current, and transition facts coexist and mislead answers—and proposes ATMA, a state-aware overlay that manages bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer-time resolution. They introduce the LTP benchmark for evaluating ghost memory failures and show that Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 and temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705.
AI.motivation: LLM agents rely on long-term memory to act as persistent assistants, but user facts change over time. Existing memory systems fail to distinguish between current, outdated, and transition facts, leading to "ghost memory" where conflicting fact states coexist and mislead the answer model. The paper argues that memory systems lack explicit state awareness and decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer levels.
AI.method: The authors propose ATMA, a state-aware overlay that operates on three levels: (1) bank maintenance—keeps superseded and transition records; (2) retrieval—builds evidence packets for the query's requested state view; (3) answer-time resolution—exposes current, historical, and transition labels to QA. They also build LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict-heavy benchmark for ghost memory evaluation, and propose decoupled evaluation across bank, retrieval, and answer levels.
AI.result: On the LTP benchmark, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. The gains are host-dependent but demonstrate that explicit state roles reduce memory failures that are otherwise hidden by final QA accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Memory systems for LLM agents should be understood and optimized at three distinct levels—bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer-time resolution. Explicitly modeling state roles (current, historical, transition) can significantly reduce ghost memory failures. The community should adopt decoupled evaluation to avoid misleading conclusions drawn from final QA accuracy alone.

title: Atomic Task Graph: A Unified Framework for Agentic Planning and Execution
summary: LLM-based agents have shown strong potential for solving complex multi-step tasks, yet existing performance improvements often rely on either scaling to larger backbone models or task-specific fine-tuning. The former incurs substantial computational costs, while the latter typically generalizes poorly across different tasks. Although prompt-based control is training-free and broadly applicable, existing methods still leave input-output dependencies between subtasks implicit in textual trajectories, making verified intermediate results difficult to reuse. To address these limitations, we propose Atomic Task Graph (ATG), a unified control framework for planning and execution. Specifically, ATG maintains an explicit graph to expose dependencies and support reuse. During planning, it recursively decomposes a high-level task into subtasks, forming a sequence of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) whose evolution can be traced. During execution, the dependencies exposed by ATG allow independent branches to be executed in parallel, thereby improving execution efficiency. When failures are detected, ATG leverages the graph evolution history to localize the error source and repair only the affected region, preserving validated regions unchanged. Experiments show that ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks using only 7B-8B backbones.

AI.tldr: ATG is a training-free, prompt-based control framework that uses an explicit directed acyclic graph to decompose, execute, and repair multi-step tasks. It enables parallel execution, error localization, and partial repair, outperforming baselines on 7B-8B models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based agent improvements rely on scaling to larger models (costly) or task-specific fine-tuning (poor generalization). Prompt-based methods are training-free but leave subtask dependencies implicit in text, preventing verification and reuse of intermediate results.
AI.method: ATG maintains an explicit graph (DAG) to expose dependencies. Planning recursively decomposes high-level tasks into subtasks forming evolving DAGs. Execution runs independent branches in parallel. On failure, ATG uses graph evolution history to localize errors and repair only the affected region.
AI.result: ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks using only 7B-8B backbone models.
AI.conclusion: Explicit graph-based dependency tracking enables training-free, efficient, and robust multi-step agent control without requiring large models or task-specific fine-tuning.

title: OntoLearner: A Modular Python Library for Ontology Learning with Large Language Models
comment: 30 pages. Under review at Nature Communications. This version is reformatted with a different section structure; content is unchanged
summary: Ontology learning (OL) aims to automatically construct structured knowledge models from text, yet progress remains fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices. Despite decades of research, OL lacks a shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access. This absence has hindered progress and fragmented research, leaving the central challenges of OL largely unaddressed. We introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain, and first-of-its-kind framework that unifies ontology access, large language model (LLM)-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking. OntoLearner releases 180 machine-readable ontologies spanning 22 domains and provides pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for three core OL tasks: term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction. Using this infrastructure, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of OL, evaluating 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks. The results converge on a finding that reframes the central challenge of OL: failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is not model capability, but a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it. These findings establish that effective OL is reachable through the cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking enabled by OntoLearner. OntoLearner is open-source (MIT license) at https://github.com/sciknoworg/OntoLearner/.

AI.tldr: OntoLearner is a first-of-its-kind framework unifying ontology access, LLM-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking across 22 domains, revealing that OL's central bottleneck is structural mismatch between model knowledge encoding and ontological organization rather than model capability.
AI.motivation: Ontology learning research is fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices, lacking shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access, which has hindered progress and left central challenges unaddressed.
AI.method: OntoLearner provides 180 machine-readable ontologies across 22 domains, pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for three core OL tasks (term typing, taxonomy discovery, non-taxonomic relation extraction), and conducts large-scale empirical study evaluating 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks.
AI.result: Failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication; the primary bottleneck is structural mismatch between model knowledge encoding and ontological organization.
AI.conclusion: Effective OL is reachable through cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking enabled by OntoLearner, establishing that the central challenge is structural alignment rather than model capability.

title: Multimodal Knowledge Edit-Scoped Generalization for Online Recursive MLLM Editing
summary: Online multimodal knowledge editing requires injecting a continual stream of visual-textual corrections into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with bounded overhead and minimal disruption to unrelated behaviors. Existing editors mainly emphasize edit reliability and long-horizon stability, but rarely control the semantic boundary of each edit. Our pilot analyses of post-edit behaviors and internal neuronal activities reveal a scope gap behind reliable edits: instance-level success neither guarantees transfer to valid cross-modal variants nor prevents leakage to unrelated inputs, while edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers. Therefore, we formulate Edit-Scoped Generalization, reframing online MLLM editing from merely correcting an instance to controlling the propagation boundary of each edit. To this end, we propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor that decomposes each update into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch. The local branch supports stable edit absorption, whereas the shared branch enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches perform scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman--Morrison recursions, yielding constant per-edit overhead. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures show that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality, while preserving edit reliability, stability and online efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/lab-klc/ScopeEdit.

AI.tldr: ScopeEdit is a scope-aware online editor for multimodal large language models that decomposes each edit into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch, enabling controlled cross-modal propagation while preventing leakage to unrelated inputs, achieving improved trade-off between in-scope transfer and out-of-scope locality.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal editors focus on edit reliability and long-horizon stability but fail to control the semantic boundary of each edit, leading to a scope gap where instance-level success does not guarantee transfer to valid cross-modal variants nor prevent leakage to unrelated inputs.
AI.method: ScopeEdit decomposes each update into two branches: (1) a modality-local absorption branch for stable edit absorption, and (2) an evidence-gated shared generalization branch that enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches use scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces with branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman-Morrison recursions for constant per-edit overhead.
AI.result: ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures, while preserving edit reliability, stability, and online efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Online MLLM editing should be reframed from merely correcting an instance to controlling the propagation boundary of each edit, and ScopeEdit demonstrates that scope-aware editing with separated localization and generalization branches effectively addresses this challenge.

title: Traceable Fault Diagnosis for Battery Energy Storage Systems via Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent O&M Assistant
summary: Large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESSs) require O&M decisions that combine alarms, cell-level measurements, device topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents. Monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations, but they often cannot explain whether voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality needs intervention. This digest presents a traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant that uses retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to connect operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation. Reliability is improved through BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained natural-language database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis. Preliminary internal evaluation is reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.

AI.tldr: A traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant using retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning that integrates alarms, cell measurements, topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents for interpretable fault diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Existing BESS monitoring platforms can detect threshold violations but fail to explain root causes (e.g., voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, thermal abnormality), lacking interpretable O&M decision support.
AI.method: Retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning framework with BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained NL database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis.
AI.result: Preliminary internal evaluation reported for routing accuracy, database access correctness, and diagnostic reasoning quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diagnostic assistant improves explainability and reliability of BESS fault diagnosis by connecting diverse operational data with domain knowledge through multi-agent retrieval-augmented reasoning.

title: InduceKV: Fixed-Footprint Continual Adaptation of Multimodal LLMs via Inducing KV Memories
summary: Multimodal large language models must adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet continual improvement under bounded deployment footprint remains difficult because repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores can accumulate adaptation state over time. We study fixed-footprint continual adaptation: the deployed adaptation state is kept under a fixed memory budget, while the backbone model is left unchanged and task-specific updates are externalized. We propose InduceKV, a retrieval-based method that stores each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry, consisting of a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise key--value (KV) payloads that can be appended to the model's self-attention cache. Under a strict memory budget, InduceKV constructs a compact inducing set through bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration is fit for retrieval, while the selected memory balances current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space. Across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. We further report backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics, showing that the gains are not due to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool.

AI.tldr: InduceKV is a retrieval-based method for fixed-footprint continual adaptation of multimodal LLMs, using bilevel selection to construct a compact inducing set of attention-ready KV memory entries that adapt models without changing the backbone or growing memory unboundedly.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs need to continually adapt to evolving tasks and domains, but repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores accumulate state over time, making continual improvement difficult under bounded deployment footprints.
AI.method: InduceKV stores selected training prefixes as attention-ready memory entries (frozen retrieval key + compact layerwise KV payloads) appended to self-attention cache. It constructs a compact inducing set via bilevel selection: lightweight calibration for retrieval, balancing current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in frozen retrieval space.
AI.result: InduceKV consistently outperforms PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning. Gains are not due to stronger backbone, replay alone, or unbounded candidate pool.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-footprint continual adaptation is achievable via externalized, retrieval-based memory with bilevel selection, enabling effective adaptation without backbone modification or unbounded memory growth.

title: Hidden Forgetting in Continual Multimodal Learning: When Accuracy Survives but Grounding Fails
summary: Multimodal large language models must continually adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet standard continual learning metrics mainly measure whether old answers remain correct, leaving the stability of multimodal grounding largely unexamined. We study this overlooked failure mode and ask whether a continually adapted MLLM can preserve not only what it answers, but also how it uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence. We identify \emph{hidden evidence-use forgetting}, where answer accuracy is retained while the model silently shifts toward different or less grounded evidence channels, and propose \textsc{RCL}, a replay-free reliance-constrained continual learning framework. \textsc{RCL} freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation without adding inference-time cost. Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, \textsc{RCL} consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting over replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates. These results suggest that robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "hidden evidence-use forgetting" in continually adapted multimodal LLMs, where models retain answer accuracy but shift their underlying evidence reliance. The proposed RCL framework preserves both what the model answers and how it uses multimodal evidence, outperforming existing continual learning methods.
AI.motivation: Standard continual learning metrics only track whether old answers remain correct, but ignore whether multimodal grounding (how the model uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence) remains stable. This overlooked failure mode — hidden evidence-use forgetting — is the key motivation.
AI.method: RCL (Reliance-Constrained Continual Learning) freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles via counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation without inference-time cost.
AI.result: Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, RCL consistently outperforms replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines in final performance and forgetting reduction, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates.
AI.conclusion: Robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
summary: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: PACE predicts expensive agentic benchmark scores using cheap, non-agentic evaluation instances, achieving under 4% MAE and >0.80 Spearman correlation at <1% of full evaluation cost.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA is prohibitively expensive (thousands of dollars, days of compute) and requires complex infrastructure, while non-agentic benchmarks for atomic capabilities are fast and cheap. The authors aim to bridge this gap by predicting agentic performance from non-agentic evaluations.
AI.method: PACE constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting a compact subset of non-agentic evaluation instances whose aggregated scores best predict target agentic benchmark scores. It uses a regression approach (mapping source instance scores to target scores) with two complementary instance-selection strategies: target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. The result is PACE-Bench, evaluated on 4 agentic benchmarks, 14 models, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks.
AI.result: PACE-Bench achieves LOOCV mean absolute error under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. It also reveals which atomic skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands.
AI.conclusion: PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing without the overhead of full agent evaluation, making agentic benchmarking practical and cost-effective.

title: Algebraic Model Counting for Global Analysis of Optimal Decision Trees
comment: Proc. Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML-PKDD 2026), LNCS, Naples, Italy, 7-11 September 2026
summary: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space. We propose a formal framework for the exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees, called Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC). Inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation, ADTC reformulates diverse analytical tasks, such as optimization, counting, and sampling, into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring $R$. While the hypothesis space of decision trees is doubly exponential with respect to the maximum depth $Δ$, our dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity in the number of features $n$, where $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors. To handle complex constraints consisting of multiple tree metrics, we introduce model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring. This algebraic approach efficiently constructs a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness. We demonstrate the utility of our software, emtrees, on real-world datasets, illustrating how ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC), a formal framework for exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees by reformulating analytical tasks into unified sum-of-products computation over semirings, achieving O*(n^{O(Δ)}) complexity and enabling global model landscape assessment via tensor semirings.
AI.motivation: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space, which existing methods do not provide exhaustively.
AI.method: ADTC reformulates optimization, counting, and sampling tasks into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring R, inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC). It introduces model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring, and uses a dynamic programming algorithm achieving O*(n^{O(Δ)}) time complexity.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves O*(n^{O(Δ)}) time complexity in the number of features n for decision trees with maximum depth Δ, and the software emtrees demonstrates utility on real-world datasets for evidence-based model selection.
AI.conclusion: ADTC enables evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains by constructing a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness.

title: Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

AI.tldr: Maven is an RL framework with editable evidence memory that rewards intermediate evidence-state transitions (add, link, drop) rather than just final answers, outperforming baselines on long-context reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context RL methods reward final answers or static evidence extraction, lacking feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state.
AI.method: Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add (marginal gain + hindsight contribution), link (evidence synergy), and drop (improved answer support after removing misleading evidence). Rewards are assigned to corresponding action spans in GRPO.
AI.result: Outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention.
AI.conclusion: Long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

title: SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking
summary: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

AI.tldr: SUNTA uses prediction-error-driven (surprise-based) chunking in hierarchical state-space models to improve long-horizon video prediction, employing a decoupled training strategy and internal inconsistency as a surprise metric to avoid hierarchical collapse and enable open-loop prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing HSSMs rely on fixed-length or similarity-based chunking that misaligns with data's temporal structure; the authors argue chunking should be driven by prediction errors (surprise) as they directly indicate when longer-range context is needed.
AI.method: SUNTA introduces (1) a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and avoid hierarchical collapse, and (2) internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries during imagined rollouts (open-loop prediction).
AI.result: On 2D and 3D video prediction tasks, SUNTA maintains accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, while all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.
AI.conclusion: Surprise-based temporal abstraction with decoupled training enables far more robust long-horizon prediction in HSSMs compared to existing chunking methods.

title: ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent
summary:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

AI.tldr: ContextNext is an open specification and reference implementation for governed, AI-consumable knowledge vaults that adds a governance layer beneath retrieval—ensuring artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before RAG systems operate over them. Experiments show it Pareto-dominates BM25 in stale-version attacks (97% vs 93-90% pass rate at 1/3 token cost) and provides deterministic retrieval (Jaccard 1.0) where dense+HNSW is non-deterministic (mean Jaccard 0.611).
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents rely on external knowledge stores that provide relevance but lack durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction—a gap formalized as context governance.
AI.method: The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes via MCP, and audit traces of agent context consumption.
AI.result: Governed selection achieves 97% answer-quality pass rate vs 93-90% for BM25 at ~1/3 the input-token cost in stale-version attacks. Deterministic selectors yield Jaccard 1.0 across repeated queries vs dense+HNSW at mean Jaccard 0.611 (80% queries non-deterministic).
AI.conclusion: Context governance addresses failure modes that retrieval quality alone cannot resolve; the core engine, CLI, and MCP server are released under open licenses.

title: Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training
comment: 8 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures. Accepted by the 12th International Conference on Big Data Computing and Communications (BigCom 2026)
summary: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

AI.tldr: FitOne is a series of domain-specific fitness LLMs (8B/32B parameters) built upon Qwen3 via a three-stage post-training pipeline (continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning), achieving ~10-13% improvement on professional fitness certification exams (ACSM-EP, NSCA-CSCS) while retaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) delivered by human professionals is costly and inaccessible. General-purpose LLMs lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. The goal is to develop more reliable and specialized fitness LLMs for inclusive fitness coaching.
AI.method: FitOne is developed upon Qwen3 foundation models through a three-stage post-training pipeline: (1) continual pre-training, (2) supervised fine-tuning, and (3) reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. Two model sizes are produced: 8B and 32B parameters.
AI.result: FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% on ACSM-EP and 12.73%/7.01% on NSCA-CSCS exams compared to Qwen3 base models, while retaining strong general capabilities in knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage pipeline effectively balances domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. This research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and inspires future work on developing domain-specific LLMs.

title: Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers
summary: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

AI.tldr: Paper-replication is a workflow implemented as a coding-agent skill that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, enabling automated replication of computational claims from scientific machine learning papers.
AI.motivation: Coding agents prompted to replicate paper claims do not reliably preserve progress or verify whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims, motivating a structured workflow for target-driven replication.
AI.method: The workflow records targets, reconstructs the paper's method, runs experiments, links outputs to provenance and comparisons with claims, records where evidence appears in the report, and passes validation checks before completion.
AI.result: Evaluated on twelve runs across four papers: all workspaces passed the completion gate, all 158 targets matched with report coverage. Runs varied in target division, numerical fidelity, replication time, intermediate executions, and evidence acceptance rules.
AI.conclusion: Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than the agent's final message, providing a more robust framework for automated replication.

title: A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction
summary: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

AI.tldr: A2utoLPBench is a generator-based benchmark for LLM-driven agents solving linear programming word problems, offering unlimited fresh problems, adjustable difficulty, ground-truth answers by construction, and resistance to data leakage.
AI.motivation: Existing LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets with fixed size, difficulty, and susceptibility to training-data leakage into LLMs.
AI.method: Problems are generated by first picking a feasible point and dual, then constructing a problem where that point is optimal with known objective value. A Docker-based evaluation environment with a solver-critic baseline is provided.
AI.result: The benchmark provides unlimited fresh problems, adjustable difficulty via (n,m) parameters, correct-by-construction answers, low cost per problem, repeatable scores, and resistance to data leakage using post-cutoff seed ranges.
AI.conclusion: A2utoLPBench overcomes fundamental limitations of static datasets for evaluating LLMs on linear programming tasks.

title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
summary: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios with MECE rubrics reveal frontier LLMs fail critically: top models pass only 32-42% of high-weight criteria, while 52% of critical criteria are unmet by any model, despite 80-90% pass rates on low-weight items.
AI.motivation: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are saturated and fail to capture real clinical reasoning; open-ended clinical performance remains poor (HealthBench Hard top score 32%). A more rigorous, clinically-grounded evaluation is needed.
AI.method: Five expert-authored clinical scenarios (4 specialties) with atomic, weighted MECE rubrics (184 criteria total). Three frontier LLMs (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) evaluated. Three LLM autoraters validated for rubric grading accuracy.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical weight-5 criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7% vs. 80-90% for weight-1. 52% of critical criteria satisfied by no model. Autoraters reproduced 92.8-94.7% of expert labels.
AI.conclusion: There is a systematic inversion of clinical priority in LLM performance — models fail on high-stakes items while succeeding on low-stakes ones. The pipeline is scalable and ready for large-benchmark development.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

AI.tldr: UA-ChatDev integrates uncertainty quantification into multi-agent software development to mitigate hallucination propagation, outperforming existing frameworks on the SRDD benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent software development frameworks assume all intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, making them vulnerable to hallucination propagation where incorrect early-phase decisions degrade downstream software quality.
AI.method: UA-ChatDev uses token-level log probability-based uncertainty estimation with phase-aware threshold calibration to trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels.
AI.result: Outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent frameworks on SRDD benchmark across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality; ablation studies confirm uncertainty-aware interactions improve code execution reliability.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware agent interactions effectively mitigate hallucination propagation and enhance software quality in multi-agent development pipelines.

title: Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks
summary: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

AI.tldr: Proposes Guard Rail Validation (GRV), a runtime framework that intercepts and validates AI/ML agent decisions in autonomous telecom networks before execution, using multi-dimensional criticality scoring and graduated validation mechanisms.
AI.motivation: No standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual AI inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes in autonomous networks (Levels 4-5), creating risks of erroneous decisions without human oversight.
AI.method: GRV evaluates decisions across six weighted dimensions (action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, temporal patterns) to determine criticality, then applies graduated validation: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. Includes cross-agent conflict detection and runtime conformance logging.
AI.result: Presents architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluates threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.
AI.conclusion: GRV provides a standardizable runtime safety layer for autonomous telecom networks, enabling safe AI-driven operations with regulatory compliance support (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14).

title: Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

AI.tldr: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) fails on long chain-of-thought reasoning models because the teacher's supervision is dominated by reference-induced shortcuts. The authors propose a two-step solution: isolating the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component by subtracting a reference-only teacher signal, and using pointwise mutual information (PMI) to filter out non-transferable shortcuts. Experiments show consistent improvements over base models and standard OPSD while preserving epistemic behavior.
AI.motivation: OPSD, though promising for improving LLM reasoning, consistently fails on long-CoT reasoning models—destabilizing their reflective reasoning capability and yielding marginal gains at best. The authors aim to diagnose and fix this failure.
AI.method: (1) Decompose the teacher's supervision signal to identify that the reference-induced component dominates and drives rote memorization. (2) Construct a reference-only teacher (same model conditioned on reference without question) to isolate the non-transferable component; subtract it from the full signal. (3) Use pointwise mutual information (PMI) to transform the residual into a well-formed target distribution for distillation.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD across four long-CoT models and two datasets, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.
AI.conclusion: The identified root cause (reference-induced shortcut domination) and the proposed two-step solution (reference-only subtraction + PMI-based distillation) effectively fix OPSD's failure on long-CoT models, enabling reliable self-distillation for long-chain reasoning.

title: Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support
summary: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

AI.tldr: Copewell is a multi-agent swarm system that expands access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI, featuring multi-source assessment, valence-arousal emotion mapping, and dual-mode intervention delivery with ethical oversight.
AI.motivation: Nearly one billion people globally suffer from mental health disorders, yet 75% in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Existing AI wellness solutions rely on single-mode conversational interfaces with high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief adapted to dynamic emotional states.
AI.method: The paper presents Copewell, a multi-agent swarm system with three technical innovations: (1) multi-source assessment integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model for routing users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. Sociotechnical design includes privacy-first architecture, an Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design with practitioners.
AI.result: Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a bounded memory contract for long-horizon LLM agents, using typed retrieval instead of raw transcript concatenation. Tested on Slay the Spire 2, their ablation shows strategic skills improve win rate from 3/10 to 6/10 (directional). They release a reproducible benchmark with 298 trajectories.
AI.motivation: Standard long-context LLM agents concatenate all past observations into a jumbled prompt, making it hard to isolate effects of individual memory components. The authors aim to design a bounded, structured memory contract that supports controlled ablation studies.
AI.method: They propose a bounded contract where each decision uses a fresh user message assembled via typed retrieval, not raw cross-decision transcript. They implement this in Slay the Spire 2, with a fixed-A0 ablation comparing no-store baseline (3/10 wins) vs. strategic skill layer (6/10 wins), and also report cross-backbone probes and accumulating-context baselines.
AI.result: Adding strategic skills yields a directional improvement from 3/10 to 6/10 wins (Fisher exact p≈0.37, not statistically significant). Public benchmark of frontier LLMs reports zero wins at lowest difficulty; developer-reported human win rate is 16%. The task is hard but not saturated.
AI.conclusion: The bounded memory contract enables isolated ablation of memory layers in long-horizon LLM agents. The authors release a reproducible testbed with 298 trajectories, frozen snapshots, and analysis scripts for studying how explicit memory layers shape agent decisions.

title: A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets
summary: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

AI.tldr: HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) enhances linear-attention models with a bounded exact KV cache acting as a hippocampal complement, improving long-context recall and perplexity by storing associations that would otherwise be overwritten in the compressive state.
AI.motivation: Linear-attention and state-space models compress prefixes into a fixed-size recurrent state, achieving O(1) memory but suffering from lossy exact memory—when many key-value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades.
AI.method: HOLA keeps the usual delta-rule state as compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache (semiparametric test-time memory). The cache writes without a learned eviction module, retaining tokens with large β·‖e‖ (prediction residual committed to the state). A decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read enables sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging.
AI.result: At 340M parameters trained on 15B tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26, achieves best linear in-context retrieval, and remains robust on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x training length).
